subject: Endocrine
vignette: A 28-year-old woman has 3 months of palpitations, heat intolerance, and unintentional weight loss despite an increased appetite. Examination shows a diffusely enlarged thyroid gland, bilateral proptosis, and a painless boggy swelling over the shins. Laboratory studies show TSH <0.01 mIU/L and elevated free T4.
question: Which of the following best explains the pathophysiology of her thyroid disease?

options.text: Autoimmune destruction of thyroid follicular cells by cytotoxic T lymphocytes
Autonomous functioning thyroid nodules operating independently of TSH
IgG autoantibodies binding to and stimulating TSH receptors on follicular cells
Amyloid deposition from proliferation of parafollicular C cells
Exogenous ingestion of excess thyroid hormone for weight loss

explanation_correct: Graves disease is the most common cause of hyperthyroidism and is mediated by thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin (TSI), an IgG that binds and activates TSH receptors on thyroid follicular cells. This produces diffuse goiter with increased T3/T4 and suppressed TSH. It is a type II (antibody-mediated) hypersensitivity reaction, and the antibody can cross the placenta to cause transient neonatal hyperthyroidism. The same antibody stimulates dermal fibroblasts (pretibial myxedema) and orbital fibroblasts (orbitopathy), explaining her shin and eye findings.

explanation_incorrect.A: Cytotoxic T-cell destruction of follicles is Hashimoto thyroiditis, which causes hypothyroidism rather than hyperthyroidism and lacks orbitopathy.
explanation_incorrect.B: Autonomous hyperfunctioning patches describe toxic multinodular goiter, which produces a nodular rather than diffuse gland and no pretibial or orbital findings.
explanation_incorrect.D: Parafollicular C-cell proliferation with amyloid stroma is medullary carcinoma, which does not cause diffuse hyperthyroidism with exophthalmos.
explanation_incorrect.E: Exogenous hormone ingestion suppresses the gland and would not produce a diffuse goiter, proptosis, or pretibial myxedema.

educationalObjective: Graves disease results from TSH-receptor–stimulating IgG (TSI), a type II hypersensitivity reaction that causes diffuse goiter, orbitopathy, and pretibial myxedema.

subject: Endocrine
vignette: A 34-year-old woman with Graves disease develops progressive bilateral proptosis. Biopsy of retroorbital tissue shows lymphocytic infiltration, and cytokine analysis demonstrates elevated TNF-alpha and IFN-gamma. She is euthyroid after antithyroid therapy but the eye findings continue to worsen.
question: Which of the following best describes the sequence of events that produces exophthalmos in this patient?

options.text: Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin directly stimulates orbital adipocytes to proliferate without any cytokine involvement
T-cell activation causes retroorbital lymphocytic infiltration, cytokine release, fibroblast GAG secretion, and osmotic muscle swelling with increased adipocytes
A TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma raises TSH and causes retroorbital edema
Amyloid deposition from medullary thyroid carcinoma infiltrates the extraocular muscles
Cholesterol emboli to the ophthalmic artery produce retroorbital fibrosis

explanation_correct: In Graves orbitopathy, T-cell activation leads to lymphocytic infiltration of the retroorbital space. These cells release cytokines such as TNF-alpha and IFN-gamma, which stimulate orbital fibroblasts to secrete hydrophilic glycosaminoglycans (GAGs). The GAGs draw water osmotically, producing muscle swelling, muscle inflammation, and an increased adipocyte count, which together cause exophthalmos. The orbitopathy is treated with glucocorticoids and is distinct from the TSH-receptor antibody effect on the thyroid gland itself.

explanation_incorrect.A: Orbital fibroblasts and T-cell-derived cytokines, not direct antibody stimulation of adipocytes, drive the GAG deposition and swelling.
explanation_incorrect.C: A TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma raises TSH and free T4 but does not produce retroorbital lymphocytic infiltration or the described cytokine cascade.
explanation_incorrect.D: Amyloid stroma is the hallmark of medullary carcinoma, not of Graves eye disease, and would not produce the cytokine-rich infiltrate described.
explanation_incorrect.E: Cholesterol emboli are not part of Graves pathophysiology and would not cause a lymphocytic retroorbital infiltrate.

educationalObjective: Graves exophthalmos results from T-cell–mediated retroorbital inflammation with cytokine-driven fibroblast GAG secretion and osmotic swelling.

subject: Endocrine
vignette: A 24-year-old woman with palpitations and weight loss has a suppressed TSH and a high free T4. A thyroid biopsy is performed. Microscopy shows tall, crowded follicular epithelial cells with scalloped edges of the colloid.
question: Which of the following diagnoses is most consistent with these histologic findings?

options.text: Graves disease
Hashimoto thyroiditis
Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis
Follicular carcinoma
Medullary carcinoma

explanation_correct: Tall, crowded follicular epithelial cells with scalloped colloid are the classic histologic appearance of Graves disease. The scalloping reflects active resorption of colloid by intensely stimulated follicular cells, and the tall crowded cells reflect TSH-receptor activation by thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin. This appearance pairs with the clinical picture of diffuse goiter and hyperthyroidism.

explanation_incorrect.B: Hashimoto thyroiditis shows dense lymphocytic infiltration with germinal centers and Hurthle cells, not tall crowded follicular cells.
explanation_incorrect.C: Subacute granulomatous thyroiditis is characterized by granulomas with giant cells and follicular disruption, not scalloped colloid.
explanation_incorrect.D: Follicular carcinoma shows uniform follicles with capsular and vascular invasion rather than hyperplastic crowded cells.
explanation_incorrect.E: Medullary carcinoma consists of sheets of polygonal cells in an amyloid stroma, not follicular epithelium with scalloped colloid.

educationalObjective: Tall, crowded follicular cells with scalloped colloid on histology are characteristic of Graves disease.

subject: Endocrine
vignette: A 62-year-old woman with a long-standing goiter develops palpitations and a 5-kg weight loss over 2 months. TSH is suppressed and free T4 and T3 are elevated. Radioactive iodine scanning shows two focal areas of increased uptake within a multinodular gland and suppressed uptake elsewhere. There is no exophthalmos or pretibial myxedema.
question: Which of the following best characterizes the hyperthyroidism in this patient?

options.text: Diffuse, symmetric uptake throughout the gland caused by thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin
Autoimmune follicular destruction with release of preformed hormone
Exogenous thyroid hormone taken surreptitiously for weight loss
Focal hyperfunctioning follicular-cell patches acting independently of TSH, often from TSH-receptor mutations
Parafollicular C-cell proliferation producing excess calcitonin

explanation_correct: Toxic multinodular goiter is composed of focal patches of hyperfunctioning follicular cells distended with colloid that operate independently of TSH; TSH-receptor mutations are found in about 60% of cases. These patches appear as hot nodules on radioactive iodine scan with suppressed uptake in the surrounding gland, and hot nodules are rarely malignant. The focal uptake and absence of orbitopathy or pretibial myxedema distinguish this from Graves disease.

explanation_incorrect.A: Diffuse symmetric uptake from thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin is Graves disease, not the focal hyperfunction of a multinodular gland.
explanation_incorrect.B: Follicular destruction with hormone release describes subacute or silent thyroiditis, which would show low rather than focally increased radioiodine uptake.
explanation_incorrect.C: Exogenous thyroid hormone would suppress uptake throughout the entire gland and would not create discrete hot nodules.
explanation_incorrect.E: Parafollicular C-cell proliferation is medullary carcinoma and does not cause thyrotoxicosis or focal hot nodules.

educationalObjective: Toxic multinodular goiter causes hyperthyroidism from autonomous TSH-independent hyperfunctioning patches that appear as hot, rarely malignant nodules on radioiodine scan.

subject: Endocrine
vignette: A 45-year-old man with known Graves disease stopped taking his antithyroid medication 3 weeks ago. He presents with high fever, severe agitation, profuse diarrhea, and a rapid irregular heartbeat. Laboratory studies show elevated liver enzymes. He becomes comatose shortly after arrival.
question: Which of the following identifies the most likely cause of death and the appropriate acute treatment regimen for this patient?

options.text: Congestive heart failure; treated with propranolol and propylthiouracil alone
Status epilepticus; treated with diazepam and phenytoin
Overwhelming sepsis; treated with antibiotics and glucocorticoids alone
Respiratory failure; treated with intubation and potassium iodide alone
Tachyarrhythmia; treated with a beta blocker, propylthiouracil, glucocorticoids, and potassium iodide

explanation_correct: Thyroid storm occurs when hyperthyroidism is incompletely treated or untreated and the patient then faces acute stress such as infection, trauma, or surgery. Manifestations include agitation, delirium, fever, diarrhea, coma, and tachyarrhythmia, with the tachyarrhythmia being the classic cause of death; elevated LFTs may also be seen. Management uses the 4 P's: beta blockers (eg, propranolol), propylthiouracil, glucocorticoids (eg, prednisolone), and potassium iodide (Lugol iodine). The iodide load decreases T4 synthesis and release through the Wolff-Chaikoff effect.

explanation_incorrect.A: Tachyarrhythmia, rather than heart failure, is the classic cause of death, and therapy requires all four agents rather than only two.
explanation_incorrect.B: Seizures are not the characteristic terminal event of thyroid storm, and anticonvulsants are not its primary therapy.
explanation_incorrect.C: Infection may precipitate the storm, but death results from uncontrolled thyrotoxicosis; antibiotics and steroids alone are inadequate.
explanation_incorrect.D: Respiratory failure is not the classic cause of death, and iodide by itself is insufficient therapy for thyroid storm.

educationalObjective: Thyroid storm is a stress-precipitated hyperthyroid emergency in which tachyarrhythmia is the cause of death and treatment requires the 4 P's, including iodide-induced Wolff-Chaikoff effect.

subject: Endocrine
vignette: A 30-year-old woman presents with palpitations, weight loss, and anxiety. Her thyroid gland is normal in size and there is no exophthalmos. TSH is suppressed and free T4 and T3 are elevated. She admits to taking an inexpensive pill she purchased online to help with weight loss.
question: Which of the following is the most likely explanation for her thyrotoxicosis?

options.text: Graves disease mediated by thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin
Exogenous thyroid hormone ingestion
Toxic multinodular goiter with autonomous nodules
Struma ovarii with ectopic thyroid production
A TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma

explanation_correct: Exogenous thyrotoxicosis results from excessive intake of thyroid hormone and should be suspected in a patient trying to lose weight, especially when the gland is normal-sized and there is no goiter or orbitopathy. The ingested hormone raises free T4/T3 and suppresses TSH. This contrasts with endogenous causes such as Graves disease, in which a diffuse goiter and autoimmune findings would be expected.

explanation_incorrect.A: Graves disease would produce a diffuse goiter and often proptosis or pretibial myxedema, none of which are present here.
explanation_incorrect.C: Toxic multinodular goiter would show a nodular gland with focal hot nodules on scanning rather than a normal-sized thyroid.
explanation_incorrect.D: Struma ovarii is ectopic thyroid tissue within an ovarian teratoma and would be suggested by a pelvic mass, not a weight-loss pill.
explanation_incorrect.E: A TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma would produce an elevated or inappropriately normal TSH with high free T4, not a suppressed TSH.

educationalObjective: In a patient without goiter taking a weight-loss pill, suppressed TSH with elevated thyroid hormone suggests exogenous thyrotoxicosis.

subject: Endocrine
vignette: A 50-year-old man has a single painless nodule in the left thyroid lobe. He is euthyroid with a normal TSH. Radioactive iodine scanning shows the nodule is cold with normal uptake in the remainder of the gland. Fine-needle aspiration reveals uniform follicles without capsular or vascular invasion.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis of this nodule?

options.text: Follicular carcinoma with capsular invasion
Toxic multinodular goiter with multiple hyperfunctioning nodules
Thyroid adenoma, a benign solitary nonfunctional nodule
Graves disease with a smooth diffuse goiter
Papillary carcinoma with psammoma bodies

explanation_correct: Thyroid adenoma is a benign solitary growth of the thyroid. Most adenomas are nonfunctional and therefore appear cold on radioactive iodine scanning, although they rarely become toxic and hot through autonomous hormone production. The most common histology is follicular, and the absence of capsular or vascular invasion distinguishes it from follicular carcinoma. A cold nodule is one of the nodular causes of goiter.

explanation_incorrect.A: Follicular carcinoma invades the tumor capsule and vasculature and would not be a noninvasive follicular lesion on histology.
explanation_incorrect.B: Toxic multinodular goiter produces multiple hot nodules in a multinodular gland with suppressed background uptake, not a single cold nodule.
explanation_incorrect.D: Graves disease produces a smooth, diffuse goiter with high diffuse uptake rather than a discrete cold nodule.
explanation_incorrect.E: Papillary carcinoma would show empty Orphan Annie nuclei, nuclear grooves, and psammoma bodies rather than uniform follicles.

educationalObjective: A benign thyroid adenoma is a solitary, usually cold nodule with follicular histology that lacks capsular or vascular invasion.
